assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on the magic-wavelength idea and Sr/Yb lattice demonstrations, brought fractional uncertainties to the 1e-18 level and turned frequency measurement into a tool for geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and searches for new physics. Exactly the kind of measurement advance that opens new ways of observing nature, with an unambiguous, clearly defined invention and extensive experimental demonstration.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first Sr lattice clock; Ye drove the systematic-uncertainty and coherence record-setting work and the many-body clock. Two laureates give a clean and natural configuration. Other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Yb groups at NIST, JILA collaborators, Hollberg/Wineland-school ion clock work) overlap but are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Mature: multiple independent labs worldwide operate lattice clocks, comparisons agree, and a redefinition of the SI second is being discussed. Recognition is timely, with the Hall/Hänsch comb prize (2005) and Wineland ion-clock prize (2012) already awarded in the neighbouring area.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for ion-clock and quantum control methods could be argued as the field already being recognised.
Whether the committee would want a third name (e.g. a clock-comparison or theory contributor) is not supported by the supplied credit.
Precise priority details of the magic-wavelength proposal are from my own recollection and not independently verified here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ti:sapphire gain media, Kerr-lens mode locking and semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors (SESAMs) made reliable, compact femtosecond sources that underpin attosecond science, frequency combs, multiphoton microscopy, spectroscopy and countless time-resolved measurements. Instrument-level impact that enabled several other Nobel-recognised fields is exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Moulton for the Ti:sapphire laser material and laser, Sibbett's group for Kerr-lens mode locking, Keller for SESAM-enabled passive mode locking and high-power ultrafast oscillators. A three-person split is plausible but the decisive Kerr-lens credit is shared among several people (Sibbett's group, Spence/Kean et al.), so the allocation is somewhat contestable.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, decades of use; if anything recognition is late. Chirped pulse amplification (2018) is adjacent, which could be seen either as a precedent or as reduced room.
uncertainties: Distribution of credit between Kerr-lens mode locking contributors is genuinely disputed.
Committee might regard the area as largely covered by the 2018 and 2023 laser prizes.
Whether this is physics discovery or engineering invention needs discussion, though the Nobel statutes allow inventions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought strong light-matter coupling to superconducting circuits, providing dispersive qubit readout, coupling buses and the architecture used by nearly all superconducting quantum processors. A concrete, experimentally validated framework in which the coherence and readout figures of merit improved by orders of magnitude.
assessment.attribution: Blais and colleagues supplied the 2004 theory proposal, Wallraff and Schoelkopf the first strong-coupling experiments with Yale's team. The three-person configuration is natural; Girvin and others also contributed to the proposal but are not among the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense of two decades of independent confirmation and widespread adoption. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits reduces but does not remove the room for a related prize; timing question is whether the committee wants a second superconducting-circuit prize soon.
uncertainties: Close adjacency to the recent 2025 superconducting-circuit prize.
Credit for the original proposal beyond Blais (Girvin, Huang, Majer, Schuster) is not captured by the credited names.
Practical quantum advantage remains unproven, though the physics prize does not depend on it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade-based control of individual neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays gave programmable quantum simulators and gate-based processors with tens to hundreds of qubits, exposing new quantum many-body phases and high-fidelity entangling gates. Strong blend of precision atomic control and quantum information, and one of the fastest-moving experimental fields.
assessment.attribution: Saffman contributed the blockade-gate proposal and gate demonstrations, Browaeys the early tweezer-array and spin-model experiments, Lukin the large programmable arrays and many-body studies. Others (Bernien, Endres, Weiss, Jaksch, Zoller) also made decisive contributions, so a three-name list is a reduction.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing with independent groups reproducing key results, but the field is still evolving and the ultimate role in quantum computing is open. Probably somewhat early.
uncertainties: Premature relative to long-term stability of the field.
Attribution among Lukin, Browaeys, Saffman, Weiss, Endres, Greiner and Zoller is not straightforward.
Fidelity and scalability claims are evolving.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single spins in diamond (NV centres) and related defects gave room-temperature solid-state qubits and nanoscale quantum sensors of magnetic field, temperature and strain, with applications from condensed-matter imaging to biology. Strong quantum-sensing link and close to my own work with coherent solid-state emitters and measurement-limited science.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated optically detected magnetic resonance on single NV centres and coherent control; Awschalom extended coherent spin control to defects such as SiC and diamond. Lukin is credited as a fourth name for quantum sensing and register ideas, but only three can be selected; Lukin may arguably be more decisive than Awschalom, making the fair configuration debatable.
assessment.maturity: Largely mature for single-NV control, with independent confirmation across many labs; quantum-sensing applications are still developing, so some of the impact is prospective.
uncertainties: Four credited names for at most three prize slots with a contested choice.
Compound discovery: single-spin detection, quantum sensing and defect qubits might merit different recognition.
Strength of eventual real-world impact beyond research labs is still being demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the Jaksch-Zoller Bose-Hubbard proposal to the superfluid to Mott transition and quantum gas microscopes, gave a controllable platform for many-body physics with direct observation of correlations. Clear scientific impact and strong experimental demonstration.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are theory pioneers of the proposals, Bloch and Greiner the experimental leaders (Greiner/Hänsch/Bloch Mott transition, microscopes). Four names compete for three slots, and Cirac/Zoller also appear on other candidates, so a prize split between theory and experiment is hard to settle.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely reproduced for over 20 years; adjacent to the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize, which may reduce room.
uncertainties: Which of Greiner and Bloch is credited, and how Hänsch/Esslinger and Jaksch fit, is unclear.
Cirac and Zoller overlapping with other candidates complicates configuration across the whole list.
Mostly analog simulation; concrete scientific discoveries beyond demonstrations may be judged modest.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Pulsar timing arrays use decades of sub-microsecond timing of millisecond pulsars as a galaxy-sized detector. Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background opens a new frequency window, a remarkable precision-measurement achievement.
assessment.attribution: Evidence came from several collaborations (NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, CPTA, InPTA). The credited three are leaders of different collaborations and the Hellings-Downs correlation, timing methodology and pulsar discoveries have many other authors; a fair three-person prize is hard to define.
assessment.maturity: Premature: the 2023 results are a few-sigma evidence for the Hellings-Downs signature, and the astrophysical origin (supermassive black hole binaries versus new physics) is not settled. Waiting for a firm detection is prudent.
uncertainties: Significance below conventional discovery threshold and interpretation of the source open.
Collaboration structure makes individual attribution difficult.
Credit for the underlying pulsar timing methods and detector concept is spread across more people than credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The qPlus tuning-fork sensor and CO-functionalised tips gave atomic-resolution force microscopy, including imaging of molecular bond structure. A measurement method that opened a new way to see matter at the single-bond level, and which has been adopted widely in surface science and on-surface chemistry.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl invented the qPlus sensor and developed frequency-modulation AFM at atomic resolution; Gross and Meyer (IBM Zurich) demonstrated sub-molecular bond-resolved imaging with functionalised tips. The split between instrument invention and a landmark demonstration is plausible, but it is a smaller community than other candidates and AFM itself (Binnig, Quate, Gerber) is a prior invention.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced in many labs, though the overall field impact is narrower than the top-ranked candidates.
uncertainties: Breadth of scientific impact beyond surface science and chemistry is limited compared to other candidates.
Relationship to the STM/AFM prize heritage and to Binnig's AFM invention.
The role of the broader community (e.g. Albrecht, Hembacher, Welker) is not captured.
